proposals.quote_modern: they all made an excellent dinner
proposals.replacement: they all had an excellent dinner
proposals.butler: they all made an excellent dinner
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶7 'made an excellent dinner' (syntax, pause, high): read as 'Ate an excellent dinner (not cooked one)'; note 'Old idiom'. The reader had to rule out the cooking sense explicitly.
proposals.reason: False friend. In current English to 'make dinner' is to cook it (this Book itself says 'prepare an excellent dinner' for the maids' cooking at ¶32), so a present-day reader's first reading is that the company cooked the meal the carvers have just served out. Butler's idiom 'make a good dinner' means to eat one. 'had' is the plain current verb for the same act; 'all', 'excellent' and 'dinner' stay. Recoverable from the carvers handing out portions, hence optional.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶7 has 'had' four times: as an auxiliary, and as the main verb in 'had had enough to eat and drink', which is the same sense of eating as the repair, so no Butler word is reused for something else. His other 'made' ('made an end of praying') is already 'finished' and is not affected. If the lead dislikes 'had … had had', 'ate' is equally safe: Butler's 'eat' in the next sentence has the same sense.

proposals.quote_modern: by the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife
proposals.replacement: by the treachery of Aegisthus and his own wife
proposals.butler: as Agamemnon was by the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶19 'Aegisthus and his wife' (relationship, MISREAD, medium): "'His' most naturally attaches to Aegisthus; corrected only two paragraphs later". The paraphrase hedges with quotes ('the treachery of Aegisthus and "his wife"'), and book-level note 7 calls it 'the "Aegisthus and his wife" misreading in ¶19'.
proposals.reason: The pronoun misleads on a relationship. 'his' follows 'Aegisthus', the nearest male noun, so a reader who does not know the story takes the wife to be Aegisthus's and pictures a second conspirator who does not exist, until ¶21 names 'Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra'. Butler means Agamemnon's wife: his ¶21–22 tell that story, and his Greek has the reflexive ἧς ἀλόχοιο, 'his own wife'. 'own' is the smallest change that ties the possessive back to Agamemnon, the man who was killed. It echoes Butler's own 'my own house' earlier in the same sentence and adds no fact; no word is removed or reordered. If the lead thinks 'his own' is not clear enough, the fallback is 'Agamemnon’s wife', swapping one word and adding no emphasis.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶19 has 'own' once, in 'my own house', with the same possessive-emphasis job, so the repair echoes it and does not reuse it for something else. 'treachery', 'Aegisthus', 'wife' and 'Agamemnon' are unchanged, and nothing else in the paragraph moves.

proposals.butler: Jove counselled evil against him and made it blow hard till the waves ran mountains high. Here he divided his fleet and took the one half towards Crete
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶23 'Here he divided his fleet and took the one half toward Crete' (action, unsure, medium): 'The text says he took half to Crete, then places him in Egypt with "the other five ships"; contradictory on first pass and had to reread.' Book-level note 4 adds that '¶23 also blurs which part of Menelaus's fleet he was with.'
proposals.reason: The agent is hidden. In Butler the subject carries over from the sentence before: Jove 'made it blow hard … Here he divided his fleet and took the one half towards Crete'. So it is the storm-god who splits Menelaus's fleet. Butler then says that part 'was driven on to the rocks' and that 'the other five ships … were taken by winds and seas to Egypt, where Menelaus gathered much gold'. Menelaus was therefore not with the Crete half and cannot be the one who 'took' it there. In the modern text the sentence before opens on Menelaus ('when he too could put to sea again'), and 'his fleet' fits him, so 'he' reads as Menelaus deliberately splitting his fleet and leading half to Crete. The same paragraph then contradicts that. Naming Zeus restores Butler's agent with one word, and 'his fleet' now points back to 'him' (Menelaus) in the sentence before, since Zeus has no fleet. Butler's own 'took' is kept, and nothing is added, removed or reordered. The Greek agrees: Ζεὺς … διατμήξας τὰς μὲν Κρήτῃ ἐπέλασσεν.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶23 names 'Jove' (→ Zeus) once, and it is the same god, so this is the same referent and not a collision. 'divided', 'fleet' and 'took' are Butler's own words and stay; no other Butler word is displaced or reused.

proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶23 'much gold and substance' (word, pause, high): read as 'Wealth and possessions'; note 'Archaic sense of "substance"'. Also in book-level note 5.
proposals.reason: Known example from the brief (3.23), ruled on in context. 'substance' meaning property now survives only in the set phrase 'a man of substance'. Standing alone beside 'gold', it reads as 'material' or 'stuff', so the reader has to work out that Menelaus came home rich in goods as well as gold. 'wealth' is the plain current word for Butler's sense, works with 'much' as 'substance' did, and is how the edition already renders the same Butler word at 24.31 ('wasting the substance' → 'wasting the wealth'). The companion phrase 'people of an alien speech' is kept; see rejected_barriers. The meaning can be recovered, so this is optional.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶23 also has 'treasure' ('with as much treasure as his ships could carry'). The repair does not use that word, so his 'substance' and 'treasure' stay two different words. 'wealth' does not occur anywhere in Butler's ¶23 or in the modern Book 3, and 'gold' and 'much' are unchanged.

reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.butler: He lashed the horses on and they flew forward nothing loth into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. All that day did they travel, swaying the yoke upon their necks till the sun went down
reader_errors_not_caused_by_text.why_text_is_clear: There is no switch. summary: Book 3 is already highly comprehensible. Across all 37 content paragraphs the blind reader's paraphrases match Butler; of 107 barriers only one is a misreading (¶19) and one a real confusion (¶23), and two more mark a false friend and a dead sense worth an optional fix. The remaining 103 are pauses over Butler's names and epithets, GLOSSARY formulas, ritual terms the reader followed correctly, context from Books 1–2 (the Mentor disguise, the suitors), the ¶37 boundary, and dated but transparent idioms the reader worked out, mostly with high confidence. Both real failures are pronouns that hide who acted or whose: 'Aegisthus and his wife' (¶19) reads as Aegisthus's wife, and 'Here he divided his fleet' (¶23) reads as Menelaus splitting his own fleet, which the same paragraph then contradicts. Each is repaired with one word and marked recommended. The sweep adds two optional one-word repairs: the false friend 'made an excellent dinner' (¶7, which reads today as cooking) and the dead sense 'substance' (¶23 → 'wealth', as already printed at 24.31). 'alien speech', 'Presently', 'drink offering', 'inner/outer meats', 'tongues of the victims' and 'aegis-bearing' are kept as current or easy to follow. Nothing is blocking. Two notes for the lead rather than proposals: GLOSSARY's Book 3 row still says 'willingly enough' for 'nothing loth' where the text rightly prints 'readily enough', and Book 3's 'and then' for 'whereon' predates the Book 4 'at that' row.
